items.title: Wöhler made urea without a kidney in 1828
items.claim: Chemists in the 1820s believed organic compounds — substances found in living things — required a 'vital force' to be made. In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler, trying to make ammonium cyanate from inorganic precursors, accidentally produced urea — an organic substance found in mammalian urine.
items.prompt: Why did Wöhler's accident matter so much?

options.text: It made an organic compound from purely inorganic starting materials — the first crack in the doctrine that living things were chemically inaccessible to laboratory synthesis

items.reveal_title: The vital force begins to crack
items.reveal:
Wöhler had been heating ammonium chloride with silver cyanate. The product crystallised as colourless prisms. Analysis showed it was identical to urea — excreted by mammalian kidneys and definitively 'organic'.

He wrote to Berzelius: 'I must tell you that I can prepare urea without requiring a kidney of an animal, either man or dog.'

The vital force doctrine didn't die overnight. Urea is a borderline case — small, simple. But later syntheses (Kolbe's acetic acid in 1845, Berthelot's full organic synthesis programme in the 1850s-60s, Miller-Urey's amino acid synthesis in 1953) extended the principle until vitalism was indefensible.

Organic chemistry became 'the chemistry of carbon compounds', not 'the chemistry of life'.
items.why: A single accidental synthesis began the demolition of a centuries-old philosophical boundary between living and non-living chemistry.

items.title: Haber and Bosch fed half the world (and made the explosives that killed millions)
items.claim: In 1909 Fritz Haber at Karlsruhe demonstrated lab-scale ammonia synthesis from nitrogen and hydrogen. By 1913 Carl Bosch at BASF had scaled it to industrial production. The process now feeds about half of humanity through synthetic fertilisers — and the same ammonia was the basis of WWI explosives.
items.prompt: Why is the Haber-Bosch process considered the most consequential industrial chemistry of the 20th century?

options.text: It is the cheapest reaction known

It made cheap nitrogen fertiliser, lifting the cap on global food production and supporting the population growth from 1.6 billion in 1900 to 8 billion today; without it, several billion people could not be fed
It was the first reaction to use a catalyst

items.reveal_title: Two Nobels and a moral weight
items.reveal:
N2 + 3 H2 → 2 NH3 over an iron catalyst at 400-450°C and 150-300 atm. Single-pass yield is about 15 percent; unreacted gases are recycled to give high throughput.

Haber won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The award was controversial — he had also led Germany's poison gas programme during WWI, personally supervising the first large chlorine gas attack at Ypres in 1915. His first wife Clara Immerwahr, also a chemist, killed herself in protest a week later.

Bosch won the 1931 Nobel Prize for the engineering of high-pressure synthesis. The plant scaled to feed both fertilisers (peace) and explosives (war).

The Haber-Bosch process consumes about 1-2 percent of the world's energy today and accounts for a meaningful fraction of global CO2 emissions. Replacing it with green ammonia (using renewable hydrogen) is a current frontier.
items.why: A single chemical reaction underpins modern population scale. Its history is bound up with both food security and industrial warfare.

items.title: The element you breathe and the element that protects you are the same element
items.claim: Atmospheric oxygen is O2 — diatomic, paramagnetic, essential for respiration. Ozone is O3 — pale blue, pungent, toxic at ground level, and shields the planet from UV. Both are pure oxygen.
items.prompt: Why do ozone and oxygen behave so differently?

options.text: Ozone contains a heavier isotope of oxygen
Three-atom O3 has a bent structure with delocalised pi bonding that absorbs UV strongly (200-310 nm); two-atom O2 has different MO energies and no comparable absorption
The two are not the same element after all

items.reveal:
Ozone is bent (about 117 degrees) with three resonance structures and bond order 1.5 per O-O bond. Its electronic transitions absorb the Hartley band (200-310 nm) strongly — almost all the Sun's biologically damaging UV-B and UV-C.

This is why the Montreal Protocol (1987) was such an unusually successful environmental treaty: CFCs were depleting stratospheric ozone, and replacing them has allowed the ozone layer to begin to recover.

Ground-level ozone produced by photochemical smog is toxic to lungs at parts-per-billion. Same molecule, life-saving at 30 km up, lung-damaging at the surface.
items.why: Allotropes of an element are not minor variants. They can be biologically and atmospherically opposite.
